{{nihongo|'''Kamado Shrine'''|竈門神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} located in {{ill|Dazaifu, Fukuoka|Q728218|qid=Q728218}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258|qid=Q123258}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}}). Under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=modern shrine ranking system}}, it was formerly ranked as a {{ill|Q712534|lt=Kanpei-shōsha}}, and is currently a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|ja|別表神社|mr|बेप्प्यो तीर्थ|simple|Beppyo shrine|zh|別表神社|qid=Q10898274}} of the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077}}. It is also known as “'''Hōmangū'''” and “Kamado-gū.”<ref name="地名">“Kamado Shrine” entry, *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*.</ref> {{nihongo|'''Kamado Shrine'''|竈門神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Chikuzen Province]].

== Overview ==
The shrine is located on {{ill|Mount Hōman|Q11452604|qid=Q11452604}}, which rises to the northeast of {{ill|Dazaifu, Fukuoka|Q728218|qid=Q728218}}, and its buildings are divided into two main sites:
* '''[[#Mount Hōman (Upper Shrine and Middle Shrine Ruins)|Upper Shrine]]''' – at the summit of Mount Hōman (elevation 829.6 m).
* '''[[#Mountain Foot (Lower Shrine)|Lower Shrine]]''' – at the foot of Mount Hōman.

In the past, there was also a Middle Shrine on the mountainside, but it was abolished during the Meiji period.

Because Mount Hōman lies to the northeast—the {{ill|Kimon|Q11673539|qid=Q11673539}} (demon gate)—of {{ill|Dazaifu (government)|Q144845|qid=Q144845}}, the shrine was revered as a guardian deity protecting Dazaifu. From the {{ill|Heian period|ar|فترة هييآن|ast|Periodu Heian|az|Heyan dövrü|bcl|Panahon ni Heian|bg|Хеян|bn|হেইআন যুগ|br|Marevezh Heian|ca|Període Heian|cs|Období Heian|de|Heian-Zeit|el|Περίοδος Χεϊάν|eo|Epoko Heian|es|Período Heian|eu|Heian aroa|fa|دوره هی‌آن|fi|Heian-kausi|fr|Époque de Heian|gl|Período Heian|he|תקופת הייאן|hi|हेआन काल|hr|Heian (razdoblje)|hu|Heian-kor|hy|Հեիան ժամանակաշրջան|id|Zaman Heian|it|Periodo Heian|ja|平安時代|ka|ჰეიანის პერიოდი|ko|헤이안 시대|la|Aevum Heian|lt|Hejano laikotarpis|mn|Хэйан|mr|हियन कालावधी|ms|Zaman Heian|my|ဟဲအိအန်ခေတ်|nl|Heianperiode|nn|Heian|no|Heian-perioden|oc|Epòca d'Heian|pl|Heian|ps|هېيان دوره|pt|Período Heian|ro|Perioada Heian|ru|Период Хэйан|sh|Heianski period|simple|Heian period|sk|Obdobie Heian|sl|Obdobje Heian|sq|Periudha Heian|sr|Хеиан период|sv|Heian|ta|ஹையன் காலகட்டம்|th|ยุคเฮอัง|tl|Panahong Heian|tr|Heian Dönemi|uk|Період Хейан|vi|Thời kỳ Heian|war|Panahon Heian|wuu|平安时代|zh|平安时代|zh_classical|平安朝|zh_min_nan|Heian sî-tāi|zh_yue|平安時代|qid=Q193292}} onward, {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088|qid=Q2279088}} (the syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism) progressed, and the shrine became integrated with its {{ill|Jingū-ji|Q1074971|qid=Q1074971}} temple, Daisen-ji (also known as Kamado-san-ji or Uchi-yama-ji), which was a representative {{ill|Tiantai|Q668188|qid=Q668188}} temple in western Japan.<ref name="角川"/> In addition, Mount Hōman, together with {{ill|Mount Hiko|Q3077886|qid=Q3077886}}, developed into one of the major training grounds of {{ill|Shugendō|Q1483875|qid=Q1483875}}. These Buddhist facilities were abolished in the Meiji period; however, even today there are about 40 shrines in Fukuoka Prefecture that were {{ill|Seichi junrei|Q123923583|qid=Q123923583}}-enshrined from this shrine,<ref>“Mount Hōman” entry, *Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names: Fukuoka Prefecture*.</ref> and it continues to be worshipped for faith in Mount Hōman and for matchmaking blessings.

As cultural properties, the entire Mount Hōman area including the shrine grounds is designated a national {{ill|Historic site|Q1081138|qid=Q1081138}}. In addition, wooden komainu (guardian lion-dogs) and 307 items related to mountain worship on Mount Hōman are designated cultural properties of Fukuoka Prefecture.

== About the Shrine Name ==
[[File:Homan zan 01.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{ill|Mount Hōman|Q11452604|qid=Q11452604}}<br /><small>Because of its shape, it was formerly also called “Mount Mikasa.”</small>]]
The shrine is enshrined on {{ill|Mount Hōman|Q11452604|qid=Q11452604}} (829.6 m), northeast of {{ill|Dazaifu (government)|Q144845|qid=Q144845}}. In ancient times, this mountain was known as “Mount Mikasa” and “Mount Kamado.”<ref name="宝満山">“Mount Hōman” entry, *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*.</ref> The name “Mount Mikasa” is said to derive from its hat-like shape,<ref name="神々"/> and it is also believed to have been worshipped as a {{ill|Sacred mountains|Q1595289|qid=Q1595289}} in ancient times.<ref name="角川"/>

The other name, “Mount Kamado,” appears frequently in poetry as a {{ill|Utamakura|Q1588579|qid=Q1588579}} of {{ill|Chikuzen Province|cs|Provincie Čikuzen|de|Provinz Chikuzen|es|Provincia de Chikuzen|fa|ولایت چیکوزن|fr|Chikuzen|gl|Provincia de Chikuzen|id|Provinsi Chikuzen|it|Chikuzen (provincia)|ja|筑前国|ko|지쿠젠국|lt|Čikudzeno žemė|nl|Chikuzen (provincie)|no|Chikuzen (provins)|pt|Província de Chikuzen|ru|Тикудзэн (провинция)|simple|Chikuzen Province|sk|Čikuzen (provincia)|sr|Провинција Чикузен|tr|Chikuzen (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Тікудзен|zh|筑前國|zh_min_nan|Tikuzen-kok|zh_yue|筑前國|qid=Q1047664}}.<ref name="地名"/> According to the shrine tradition recorded in the late {{ill|Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205}} text *Kamado Hōman Daibosatsu-ki*, the mountain was originally called “Buttō-san” or “Mount Mikasa,” but gained the name “Kamado” because {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}} is said to have set up a hearth (kamado) on the mountain at the time of childbirth.<ref name="宝満山"/> On the other hand, the *{{ill|Chikuzen no Kuni Zoku Fudoki|Q108571667|qid=Q108571667}}* explains the name as deriving from the mountain’s resemblance to a {{ill|Kamado|ar|كامادو|ca|Kamado|es|Kamado|ja|かまど|ka|კამადო|pt|Kamado|qid=Q12177411}}, and from the constant clouds and mist that look like rising cooking smoke.<ref name="宝満山"/> Other theories include that a {{ill|Kitchen God|Q249178|qid=Q249178}} was enshrined for the protection of Dazaifu,<ref name="神々"/> or that the name derives from “Kamado Rock” near the ninth station of the mountain.<ref name="神々"/>

The current name “Mount Hōman” is said to originate from the syncretic designation of the enshrined deity as “Hōman Daibosatsu,”<ref name="由緒書"/> with the earliest documentary appearance dating to around the late 13th century.<ref name="由緒書"/>

== Enshrined Deities ==
'''Primary deity'''
* '''{{ill|Tamayori-hime (mother of Jimmu)|Q3082751|qid=Q3082751|lt=Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto}}'''<ref>The list of deities follows the shrine’s official history.</ref>

'''Associated deities'''
* {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}}
* {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|Q317997|qid=Q317997}} – the 15th emperor, son of Empress Jingū.

Among these, Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto is considered the original enshrined deity, while Empress Jingū and Emperor Ōjin were later added.<ref name="地名"/> Sources such as the *Hakozaki Shrine Engi* regard this shrine as the aunt of the {{ill|Hachiman|Q261637|qid=Q261637}} (aunt of Emperor Ōjin and elder sister of Empress Jingū), suggesting that by at least the early {{ill|12th century|Q7061|qid=Q7061}}, the shrine had become associated with Hachiman worship.<ref name="地名"/> Scholars point out that this incorporation into the Hachiman lineage reflects the shrine’s long-standing political ties with Dazaifu.<ref name="神々"/>

On the other hand, some theories hold that the original deity implied by the shrine’s name was the hearth god {{ill|Sanbo Kojin|Q13577821|qid=Q13577821}}.<ref>{{ill|Toshio Hōga|ja|宝賀寿男|qid=Q11452691}}, “A Tentative Theory on the Location of Fumi Province,” *Kojiki no Heya*, 2002.</ref>

In medieval times the deity was also called “Hōman Daibosatsu,” and in the early modern period “Hōman Myōjin.”<ref name="国史">*Kokushi Daijiten*, entry on Kamado Shrine.</ref>

while training in the mountains, encountered Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto. He reported this to the imperial court, and the Upper Shrine was built on the summit.<ref name="由緒書"/><ref name="神々"/> The shrine regards this event as its official founding.<ref name="由緒書"/>

Although the historical accuracy of these traditions is unclear,<ref name="神々"/> investigations of foundation stones at the Lower Shrine suggest that the shrine dates back at least to the latter half of the {{ill|8th century|Q8086|qid=Q8086}}.<ref name="地名"/> In addition, many ritual artifacts—including {{ill|Haji pottery|Q5639938|qid=Q5639938}} and {{ill|Kocho Junisen|ca|Kōchō jūnisen|es|Kōchō jūnisen|ja|皇朝十二銭|ko|황조십이전|uk|Дванадцять монет давньої Японії|zh|皇朝十二錢|qid=Q11581072}}—dating from the {{ill|9th century|Q8083|qid=Q8083}} through the medieval period have been found near the Upper Shrine, indicating connections with {{ill|Dazaifu (government)|Q144845|qid=Q144845}} and the {{ill|Japanese missions to Tang China|fa|هیئت‌های اعزامی ژاپنی به تانگ چین|fr|Missions japonaises dans la Chine des Tang|id|Misi Jepang ke Tang Tiongkok|it|Missioni giapponesi nella Cina Tang|ja|遣唐使|ko|견당사|zh|遣唐使|zh_min_nan|Khián Tông sú|qid=Q262529}}.<ref name="由緒書"/><ref name="神々"/>

As reflected in shrine tradition, the history of Kamado Shrine developed in close relation to Dazaifu.<ref name="神々"/> Another theory, however, suggests that Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto was originally worshipped naturally as a {{ill|Mikumari|fr|Mikumari|ja|水分神|simple|Mikumari-no-Kami|sv|Mikumari-no-Kami|zh|水分神|qid=Q11129547}} at the sources of the Mikasa and Hōman rivers, and only later acquired political significance.<ref name="神々"/>

As can be seen in the shrine traditions, the history of this shrine developed while maintaining a deep relationship with Dazaifu <ref name="神々"/>. On the other hand, based on the character of Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto as a “{{ill|Mikumari|fr|Mikumari|ja|水分神|simple|Mikumari-no-Kami|sv|Mikumari-no-Kami|zh|水分神|qid=Q11129547|lt=deity of water}},” there is also a theory that Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto came to be enshrined naturally as the deity of the water sources of the Mikasa River and Hōman River, and that a political divine character was later bestowed upon her <ref name="神々"/>.

== General History ==
=== From the Nara period to the Heian period ===
The earliest reliable historical record related to this shrine is an entry concerning Kamadosan-ji Temple (竈門山寺; the shrine’s {{ill|Jingū-ji|Q1074971|qid=Q1074971}}) from Enryaku 22 ({{ill|803|ab|803|af|803|am|803 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|803|ar|803|ary|803|ast|803|az|803|azb|۸۰۳ (میلادی)|bcl|803|be|803|be_x_old|803|bg|803|bn|৮০৩|bpy|মারি ৮০৩|br|803|bs|803.|ca|803|cdo|803 nièng|ceb|803|ckb|٨٠٣|crh|803|cs|803|csb|803|cv|803|cy|803|da|803|de|803|el|803|eml|803|eo|803|es|803|et|803|eu|803|fa|۸۰۳ (میلادی)|fi|803|fo|803|fr|803|frr|803|fy|803|ga|803|gan|803年|gd|803|gl|803|he|803|hi|803|hr|803.|ht|803 (almanak jilyen)|hu|803|hy|803|id|803|ilo|803|io|803|is|803|it|803|ja|803年|jv|803|ka|803|kaa|803|kk|803 жыл|ko|803년|la|803|lb|803|lij|803|lmo|803|lt|803 m.|lv|803. gads|map_bms|803|mdf|803|mg|803|mhr|803|mk|803|mr|इ.स. ८०३|mrj|803 и|ms|803|mzn|۸۰۳|nah|803|nap|803|nds|803|new|सन् ८०३|nl|803|nn|803|no|803|nrm|803|nso|803|oc|803|or|୮୦୩|os|803-æм аз|pl|803|pnb|803|pt|803|qu|803|ro|803|ru|803 год|rue|803|sa|८०३|scn|803|sd|803ع|se|803|sh|803.|shn|803|si|803|sk|803|sl|803|smn|803|sq|803|sr|803|su|803|sv|803|sw|803|tg|Соли 803|th|พ.ศ. 1346|tk|803|tl|803|tly|803|tr|803|tt|803 ел|uk|803|ur|803ء|uz|803|vec|803|vi|803|war|803|wuu|803年|xmf|803|zh|803年|zh_classical|八〇三年|zh_min_nan|803 nî|zh_yue|803年|qid=Q30388}}) <ref group="原" name="延暦22">“Eizan Daishi Den,” entry for the intercalary 10th month, 23rd day of Enryaku 22 (803). Also appears in “Fusō Ryakki,” “Kongyoku Shōchūshō,” etc.</ref> <ref name="地名"/>. As this record shows, the shrine is thought to have already been in a state of {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|Q2279088|qid=Q2279088}} (syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism) by the {{ill|Nara period|Q189178|qid=Q189178}} <ref name="神々"/>.

Regarding “Kamado-no-Kami,” the earliest mention is an article from Shōwa 7 ({{ill|840|ab|840|af|840|als|840|am|840 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|840|ar|840|ary|840|ast|840|avk|840|az|840|azb|۸۴۰ (میلادی)|ban|840|bcl|840|be|840|be_x_old|840|bg|840|bn|৮৪০|bpy|মারি ৮৪০|br|840|bs|840.|ca|840|cdo|840 nièng|ceb|840|ckb|٨٤٠|crh|840|cs|840|csb|840|cv|840|cy|840|da|840|de|840|el|840|eml|840|eo|840|es|840|et|840|eu|840|fa|۸۴۰ (میلادی)|fi|840|fo|840|fr|840|frr|840|fy|840|ga|840|gan|840年|gd|840|gl|840|he|840|hi|840|hr|840.|ht|840 (almanak jilyen)|hu|840|hy|840|id|840|ilo|840|io|840|is|840|it|840|ja|840年|jv|840|ka|840|kaa|840|kk|840 жыл|ko|840년|ksh|Joohr 840|la|840|lb|840|lij|840|lmo|840|lt|840 m.|lv|840. gads|map_bms|840|mdf|840|mg|840|mhr|840|mk|840|mr|इ.स. ८४०|mrj|840 и|ms|840|mzn|۸۴۰|nah|840|nap|840|nds|840|new|सन् ८४०|nl|840|nn|840|no|840|nrm|840|nso|840|oc|840|or|୮୪୦|os|840-æм аз|pl|840|pnb|840|pt|840|qu|840|ro|840|ru|840 год|rue|840|sa|८४०|scn|840|sd|840ع|se|840|sh|840.|shn|840|si|840|sk|840|sl|840|smn|840|sq|840|sr|840|su|840|sv|840|sw|840|tg|Соли 840|th|พ.ศ. 1383|tk|840|tl|840|tly|840|tr|840|tt|840 ел|ug|840|uk|840|ur|840ء|uz|840|vec|840|vi|840|vls|840|war|840|wuu|840年|xmf|840|zh|840年|zh_min_nan|840 nî|zh_yue|840年|qid=Q29936}}) <ref group="原" name="承和7"/> noting the bestowal of the divine rank of Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade. Thereafter, the divine rank rose to Senior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade (or possibly Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade?) in Kajō 3 ({{ill|850|ab|850|af|850|als|850|am|850 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|850|ar|850|ary|850|arz|850|ast|850|avk|850|az|850|azb|۸۵۰ (میلادی)|ban|850|bcl|850|be|850|be_x_old|850|bg|850|bn|৮৫০|bpy|মারি ৮৫০|br|850|bs|850.|ca|850|cdo|850 nièng|ce|850 шо|ceb|850|ckb|٨٥٠|crh|850|cs|850|csb|850|cv|850|cy|850|da|850|de|850|el|850|eml|850|eo|850|es|850|et|850|eu|850|fa|۸۵۰ (میلادی)|fi|850|fo|850|fr|850|frr|850|fy|850|ga|850|gan|850年|gd|850|gl|850|he|850|hi|850|hr|850.|ht|850 (almanak jilyen)|hu|850|hy|850|id|850|ilo|850|io|850|it|850|ja|850年|jv|850|ka|850|kaa|850|kk|850 жыл|ko|850년|la|850|lb|850|lij|850|lmo|850|lt|850 m.|lv|850. gads|map_bms|850|mdf|850|mhr|850|mk|850|mr|इ.स. ८५०|mrj|850 и|ms|850|mzn|۸۵۰|nah|850|nap|850|nds|850|new|सन् ८५०|nl|850|nn|850|no|850|nrm|850|nso|850|oc|850|or|୮୫୦|os|850-æм аз|pl|850|pnb|850|pt|850|qu|850|ro|850|ru|850 год|rue|850|sa|८५०|scn|850|sd|850ع|se|850|sh|850.|shn|850|si|850|simple|850|sk|850|sl|850|smn|850|sq|850|sr|850|su|850|sv|850|sw|850|tg|Соли 850|th|พ.ศ. 1393|tk|850|tl|850|tly|850|tr|850|tt|850 ел|uk|850|ur|850ء|uz|850|vec|850|vi|850|vls|850|war|850|wuu|850年|xmf|850|zea|850|zh|850年|zh_min_nan|850 nî|zh_yue|850年|qid=Q30364}}) <ref group="原" name="嘉祥3"/>; Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade in Jōgan 1 ({{ill|859|Q23897|qid=Q23897}}) <ref group="原" name="貞観元"/>; Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade in Gangyō 3 ({{ill|879|ab|879|af|879|als|879|am|879 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|879|ar|879|ary|879|ast|879|avk|879|az|879|azb|۸۷۹ (میلادی)|bar|879|bcl|879|be|879|be_x_old|879|bg|879|bn|৮৭৯|bpy|মারি ৮৭৯|br|879|bs|879.|ca|879|cdo|879 nièng|ceb|879|ckb|٨٧٩|crh|879|cs|879|csb|879|cv|879|cy|879|da|879|de|879|el|879|eml|879|eo|879|es|879|et|879|eu|879|fa|۸۷۹ (میلادی)|fi|879|fo|879|fr|879|frr|879|fy|879|ga|879|gan|879年|gd|879|gl|879|he|879|hi|879|hr|879.|ht|879 (almanak jilyen)|hu|879|hy|879|id|879|ilo|879|io|879|is|879|it|879|ja|879年|jv|879|ka|879|kaa|879|kk|879 жыл|ko|879년|la|879|lb|879|lij|879|lmo|879|lt|879 m.|lv|879. gads|map_bms|879|mdf|879|mg|879|mhr|879|mk|879|mr|इ.स. ८७९|mrj|879 и|ms|879|mzn|۸۷۹|nah|879|nap|879|nds|879|new|सन् ८७९|nl|879|nn|879|no|879|nrm|879|nso|879|oc|879|or|୮୭୯|os|879-æм аз|pl|879|pnb|879|pt|879|qu|879|ro|879|ru|879 год|rue|879|sa|८७९|scn|879|sd|879ع|se|879|sh|879.|shn|879|si|879|sk|879|sl|879|smn|879|sq|879|sr|879|su|879|sv|879|sw|879|tg|Соли 879|th|พ.ศ. 1422|tk|879|tl|879|tly|879|tr|879|tt|879 ел|uk|879|ur|879ء|uz|879|vec|879|vi|879|vls|879|war|879|wuu|879年|xmf|879|zh|879年|zh_min_nan|879 nî|zh_yue|879年|qid=Q25001}}) <ref group="原" name="元慶3"/>; and Senior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade in Kanpyō 8 ({{ill|896|ab|896|af|896|als|896|am|896 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|896|ar|896|ary|896|arz|896|ast|896|avk|896|az|896|azb|۸۹۶ (میلادی)|bar|896|bcl|896|be|896|be_x_old|896|bg|896|bn|৮৯৬|bpy|মারি ৮৯৬|br|896|bs|896.|ca|896|cdo|896 nièng|ceb|896|ckb|٨٩٦|crh|896|cs|896|csb|896|cv|896|cy|896|da|896|de|896|el|896|eml|896|eo|896|es|896|et|896|eu|896|fa|۸۹۶ (میلادی)|fi|896|fo|896|fr|896|fy|896|ga|896|gan|896年|gd|896|gl|896|he|896|hi|896|hr|896.|ht|896 (almanak jilyen)|hu|896|hy|896|id|896|ilo|896|io|896|is|896|it|896|ja|896年|jv|896|ka|896|kaa|896|kk|896 жыл|ko|896년|ku|896|la|896|lb|896|lij|896|lmo|896|lt|896 m.|lv|896. gads|map_bms|896|mdf|896|mg|896|mhr|896|mi|896|mk|896|mr|इ.स. ८९६|mrj|896 и|ms|896|mzn|۸۹۶|nah|896|nap|896|nds|896|new|सन् ८९६|nl|896|nn|896|no|896|nrm|896|nso|896|oc|896|or|୮୯୬|os|896-æм аз|pl|896|pnb|896|pt|896|qu|896|ro|896|ru|896 год|rue|896|sa|८९६|scn|896|sd|896ع|se|896|sh|896.|shn|896|si|896|sk|896|sl|896|smn|896|sq|896|sr|896|su|896|sv|896|sw|896|tg|Соли 896|th|พ.ศ. 1439|tk|896|tl|896|tly|896|tr|896|tt|896 ел|uk|896|ur|896ء|uz|896|vec|896|vi|896|war|896|wuu|896年|xmf|896|zea|896|zh|896年|zh_min_nan|896 nî|zh_yue|896年|qid=Q30465}}) <ref group="原" name="寛平8"/> <ref name="地名"/>.

In addition, there is a record of offerings in Shōwa 9 ({{ill|842|Q24730|qid=Q24730}}) <ref group="原" name="承和9">“Shoku Nihon Kōki,” entry for the 3rd day of the 7th month of Shōwa 9 (842) (see Kokugakuin University “Shintō and Shrine Historical Sources Collection”).</ref> <ref name="地名"/>. In the “{{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}}” {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|abstract|Q11064932|fr|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|zh|延喜式神名帳|qid=Q11064932}} compiled in Engi 5 ({{ill|927|Q30470|qid=Q30470}}), it is listed under Mikasa District of {{ill|Chikuzen Province|cs|Provincie Čikuzen|de|Provinz Chikuzen|es|Provincia de Chikuzen|fa|ولایت چیکوزن|fr|Chikuzen|gl|Provincia de Chikuzen|id|Provinsi Chikuzen|it|Chikuzen (provincia)|ja|筑前国|ko|지쿠젠국|lt|Čikudzeno žemė|nl|Chikuzen (provincie)|no|Chikuzen (provins)|pt|Província de Chikuzen|ru|Тикудзэн (провинция)|simple|Chikuzen Province|sk|Čikuzen (provincia)|sr|Провинција Чикузен|tr|Chikuzen (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Тікудзен|zh|筑前國|zh_min_nan|Tikuzen-kok|zh_yue|筑前國|qid=Q1047664}} as “Kamado Shrine, Myōjin Taisha,” ranking it among the {{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}} <ref name="地名"/>. The reading of the shrine name at the time is generally given as “Kamato,” though some manuscripts read it as “Kamakato” <ref name="地名"/>.

Regarding the shrine buildings, records begin with a fire in Chōji 2 ({{ill|1105|Q13719|qid=Q13719}}), followed by accounts of divination and relocation, and then another fire and related petitions in Kyūju 2 ({{ill|1155|Q19650|qid=Q19650}}) <ref name="地名"/>. As for shrine administration, by Ten’en 2 ({{ill|979|Q23784|qid=Q23784}}) the Ōmiya-shi also served as the head priest of the entire mountain, but by the late 11th century Shinto and Buddhism had become unified, and the bettō (administrative head) of Ōyama-dera Temple managed the entire mountain including this shrine. In Chōji 2 (1105), {{ill|Enryaku-ji|Q917195|qid=Q917195}} and {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Q710098|qid=Q710098}} disputed over the bettōship of Ōyama-dera, the shrine’s jingū-ji <ref name="地名"/>.

In Kajō 1 ({{ill|1106|Q19508|qid=Q19508}}) <ref group="原" name="嘉承元"/>, the shrine reached the highest divine rank of Senior First Rank, and it is said that Mount Hōman was at its peak during this period <ref name="神々"/>. There are also traditions describing the shrine at that time as the “General Guardian Shrine of the Nine Provinces” <ref name="国史"/>. Furthermore, documents related to {{ill|Hachiman|Q261637|qid=Q261637}} state that Kamado-no-Kami was the aunt of Hachiman (Emperor Ōjin), pointing to the political influence of the shrine in connection with Dazaifu and its relationship with Hachiman <ref name="神々"/>.

=== From the Kamakura period onward ===
(For developments after the {{ill|Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205}}, see also the section [[#Jingū-ji|Jingū-ji Section]].)

After the Heian period, the shrine continued to be operated as a unified Shinto-Buddhist institution <ref name="角川"/>. As this progressed, from the {{ill|Muromachi period|Q334845|qid=Q334845}} onward the name “Hōman-gū” also came into use <ref name="地名"/>. Subsequently, the shrine was caught up in the warfare of the {{ill|Sengoku period|ar|فترة سينغوكو|arz|فتره سينجوكو|be|Перыяд Сэнгоку|bg|Сенгоку|bn|সেনগোকু যুগ|bo|སེན་གོའི་དུས་མཚམས་|ca|Període Sengoku|ckb|سەردەمی سێنگۆکو|cs|Období Sengoku|de|Sengoku-Zeit|eo|Epoko Sengoku|es|Período Sengoku|et|Sengoku ajastu|eu|Sengoku aroa|fa|دوره سنگوکو|fi|Sengoku-kausi|fr|Époque Sengoku|ga|Tréimhse Sengoku|glk|سنگؤکۊ زمات|he|תקופת סנגוקו|hu|Hadakozó fejedelemségek kora (Japán)|id|Zaman Sengoku|is|Sengoku-öldin|it|Periodo Sengoku|ja|戦国時代 (日本)|ka|სენგოკუს პერიოდი|kk|Сэнгоку дәуірі|ko|센고쿠 시대|lt|Sengoku laikotarpis|ms|Zaman Sengoku|nl|Sengokuperiode|no|Sengoku-perioden|pl|Sengoku (okres)|pt|Período Sengoku|ro|Perioada Sengoku|ru|Период Сэнгоку|sh|Sengoku razdoblje|simple|Sengoku period|sk|Obdobie Sengoku|sq|Periudha Sengoku|sr|Сенгоку период|sv|Sengoku|th|ยุคเซ็งโงกุ|tl|Panahong Sengoku|tr|Sengoku Dönemi|uk|Період Сенґоку|ur|سینگوکو دور|uz|Sengoku davri|vi|Thời kỳ Chiến Quốc (Nhật Bản)|wuu|战国时代（日本）|zh|战国时代 (日本)|zh_min_nan|Sengoku sî-tāi|zh_yue|戰國時代 (日本)|qid=Q204023}} and its power declined significantly <ref name="地名"/>.

Entering the {{ill|Early modern period|Q5308718|qid=Q5308718}}, the {{ill|Kobayakawa clan|Q2975298|qid=Q2975298}}, who ruled Chikuzen Province, revived it as a {{ill|Shugendō|Q1483875|qid=Q1483875}} training ground from Tenshō 15 ({{ill|1587|Q6744|qid=Q6744}}). In Keichō 2 ({{ill|1597|Q6790|qid=Q6790}}), the main hall, worship hall, lecture hall, ascetic hall, and subsidiary shrines were rebuilt <ref name="地名"/>.

Subsequently, it also received deep reverence and donations from {{ill|Kuroda Nagamasa|Q950496|qid=Q950496}}, who entered the province in Keichō 5 ({{ill|1600|Q6720|qid=Q6720}}), but in Kan’ei 18 ({{ill|1641|Q6907|qid=Q6907}}) most of the buildings were destroyed by fire <ref name="地名"/>. In Keian 3 ({{ill|1650|Q6951|qid=Q6951}}), the shrine buildings were rebuilt by {{ill|Tadayuki Kuroda|Q11678600|qid=Q11678600}}, the second lord of the {{ill|Fukuoka Domain|Q208766|qid=Q208766}} <ref name="地名"/>. Throughout the {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}, the shrine lands amounted to 50 koku <ref name="地名"/>.

With the advent of the {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}}, Buddhist elements were eliminated through the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|Q1970535|qid=Q1970535}} <ref name="角川">“Kadokawa Dictionary of Japanese Place Names: Fukuoka Prefecture,” entry for Kamado Shrine.</ref>. Under the modern shrine ranking system in Meiji 5 ({{ill|1872|Q7753|qid=Q7753}}), it was designated a {{ill|Son-sha|ja|村社|qid=Q134917284}}, and in Meiji 28 ({{ill|1895|Q7844|qid=Q7844}}) it was promoted to a {{ill|Q712534|lt=government shrine, minor}} <ref name="由緒書"/><ref name="神々"/>. After the war, it has been listed as a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|ja|別表神社|mr|बेप्प्यो तीर्थ|simple|Beppyo shrine|zh|別表神社|qid=Q10898274}} of the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077}}.

== Divine Ranks ==
Records of divine rank bestowals to “Kamado-no-Kami.”
* {{ill|Rikkokushi|Q1151168|qid=Q1151168}}

== Shrine Grounds ==
The shrine buildings consist of the Upper Shrine at the summit of {{ill|Mount Hōman|Q11452604|qid=Q11452604}} and the Lower Shrine at the mountain’s foot. As an ancient place of worship, Mount Hōman, including the shrine precincts, has been designated a national historic site <ref name="史跡">“On the designation of Mount Hōman as a National Historic Site” (Dazaifu City website).</ref>. In the past, a Middle Shrine also existed on the mountainside <ref name="由緒書">Shrine history pamphlet.</ref>.

== Mountain Foot (Lower Shrine) ==
[[File:Kamado-jinja geku honden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Lower Shrine main hall]]
The Lower Shrine is located at the foot of the mountain. The main buildings consist of the main hall, offering hall, and worship hall.

Within the precincts are remains of a foundation-stone building measuring seven bays north–south and four bays east–west, thought to be the central facility of the abandoned Kamadosan Temple <ref name="地名"/>. Roof tiles from the 8th to 12th centuries have been excavated from the site <ref name="神々"/>.

In addition, there is an off-site worship place in Kitadani, Dazaifu City, to the north <ref name="神々"/> ({{Coord|33|32|22.57|N|130|33|4.43|E|region:JP-40_type:landmark|name=Off-site Worship Place}}).

<gallery>
File:Kamado-jinja geku shamusho.JPG|Lower Shrine office
File:Kamado-jinja torii-3.JPG|Third torii gate
File:Kamado-jinja torii-2.JPG|Second torii gate
</gallery>

== Mount Hōman (Upper Shrine and Middle Shrine Ruins) ==
[[File:Kamado Shrine 02.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Upper Shrine buildings]]
The Upper Shrine is located at the summit of Mount Hōman (elevation 829.6 meters). Near the summit are said to be the grave of the monk Shinren Shōnin and the Hōjō Cave, believed to be the burial place of the enshrined deity Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto <ref name="由緒書"/>.

Remains of the Middle Shrine remain on the mountainside. It is said that the Middle Shrine once had a lecture hall, kagura hall, En no Gyōja hall, bell tower, and other buildings, but these were abolished due to the anti-Buddhist movement of the Meiji period <ref name="角川"/>.

Elsewhere in the mountains are numerous remains of monks’ quarters and Buddhist sites, preserving traces of the era of Shinto-Buddhist syncretism <ref name="由緒書"/>.

== Jingū-ji ==
This shrine once had a jingū-ji called Ōyama-dera <ref name="角川"/>. Its sect was {{ill|Tiantai|Q668188|qid=Q668188}}.

Ōyama-dera was said to have been a representative Tendai temple of western Japan <ref name="地名"/>. Its name is also recorded as Kamadosan-ji, Uchiyama-ji, or Uchizan-ji <ref name="角川"/>; however, it is not certain that these all refer to the same temple <ref name="地名"/>.

The earliest record concerning the jingū-ji is from Enryaku 22 ({{ill|803|ab|803|af|803|am|803 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|803|ar|803|ary|803|ast|803|az|803|azb|۸۰۳ (میلادی)|bcl|803|be|803|be_x_old|803|bg|803|bn|৮০৩|bpy|মারি ৮০৩|br|803|bs|803.|ca|803|cdo|803 nièng|ceb|803|ckb|٨٠٣|crh|803|cs|803|csb|803|cv|803|cy|803|da|803|de|803|el|803|eml|803|eo|803|es|803|et|803|eu|803|fa|۸۰۳ (میلادی)|fi|803|fo|803|fr|803|frr|803|fy|803|ga|803|gan|803年|gd|803|gl|803|he|803|hi|803|hr|803.|ht|803 (almanak jilyen)|hu|803|hy|803|id|803|ilo|803|io|803|is|803|it|803|ja|803年|jv|803|ka|803|kaa|803|kk|803 жыл|ko|803년|la|803|lb|803|lij|803|lmo|803|lt|803 m.|lv|803. gads|map_bms|803|mdf|803|mg|803|mhr|803|mk|803|mr|इ.स. ८०३|mrj|803 и|ms|803|mzn|۸۰۳|nah|803|nap|803|nds|803|new|सन् ८०३|nl|803|nn|803|no|803|nrm|803|nso|803|oc|803|or|୮୦୩|os|803-æм аз|pl|803|pnb|803|pt|803|qu|803|ro|803|ru|803 год|rue|803|sa|८०३|scn|803|sd|803ع|se|803|sh|803.|shn|803|si|803|sk|803|sl|803|smn|803|sq|803|sr|803|su|803|sv|803|sw|803|tg|Соли 803|th|พ.ศ. 1346|tk|803|tl|803|tly|803|tr|803|tt|803 ел|uk|803|ur|803ء|uz|803|vec|803|vi|803|war|803|wuu|803年|xmf|803|zh|803年|zh_classical|八〇三年|zh_min_nan|803 nî|zh_yue|803年|qid=Q30388}}) <ref group="原" name="延暦22"/> <ref name="角川"/>. From the foundation stones at the Lower Shrine, it is thought to have been of considerable scale by the latter half of the 8th century <ref name="角川"/>. According to records, in Enryaku 22 (803), {{ill|Saichō|Q449943|qid=Q449943}} carved four statues of the Medicine Buddha at Kamadosan-ji for the four ships bound for Tang China <ref name="神々"/>. In Shōwa 14 ({{ill|847|Q30354|qid=Q30354}}), {{ill|Ennin|Q732282|qid=Q732282}} recited sutras before the deity upon returning from China, and in Ninju 2 ({{ill|852|Q30383|qid=Q30383}}), {{ill|Enchin|Q1972505|qid=Q1972505}} did the same <ref name="地名"/>. In Shōhei 3 ({{ill|933|Q24014|qid=Q24014}}), it is said that the monk Shamyō Shōkaku built one of Enryaku-ji’s “Six Treasure Pagodas” <ref name="地名"/>.

By the mid-Heian period, and no later than Bunji 4 ({{ill|1188|Q19732|qid=Q19732}}), the temple had become integrated with Kamado Shrine and functioned as a shrine-temple <ref name="地名"/><ref name="角川"/>. Thereafter, by the end of the 11th century, Ōyama-dera temporarily became a branch temple of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Q710098|qid=Q710098}}, but in the early 12th century it became a branch of {{ill|Enryaku-ji|Q917195|qid=Q917195}} on {{ill|Mount Hiei|Q748040|qid=Q748040}} <ref name="角川"/>. As a result, the temple’s petitions reached even the central authorities in Kyoto <ref name="地名"/>. Around Kajō 1 (1106), when Kamado Shrine was granted Senior First Rank, the temple possessed numerous monks’ quarters and reached its peak together with Kamado-no-Kami <ref name="神々"/>. In the late Heian song collection “{{ill|Ryōjin Hishō|Q3010584|qid=Q3010584}},” it is praised as “the main mountain of Kamado,” one of the sacred sites of Chikuzen <ref name="地名"/>.

From the late Kamakura period into the Muromachi period, Mount Hōman became a center of Shugendō practice, forming peak-to-peak ascetic training with Mount Hiko as the Taizōkai and Mount Hōman as the Kongōkai <ref name="地名"/><ref name="神々"/>. Entering the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|Q264012|qid=Q264012}}, warfare associated with the construction of nearby castles such as Uchizan Castle and Hōman Castle led to a decline in the temple’s power <ref name="角川"/>. In Kōji 3 ({{ill|1557|ab|1557|af|1557|als|1557|am|1557 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|1557|ar|1557|ary|1557|arz|1557|ast|1557|avk|1557|az|1557|azb|۱۵۵۷ (میلادی)|bar|1557|bcl|1557|be|1557|be_x_old|1557|bg|1557|bn|১৫৫৭|bpy|মারি ১৫৫৭|br|1557|bs|1557.|ca|1557|cdo|1557 nièng|ce|1557 шо|ceb|1557|ckb|١٥٥٧|crh|1557|cs|1557|cv|1557|cy|1557|da|1557|de|1557|diq|1557|el|1557|eml|1557|eo|1557|es|1557|et|1557|eu|1557|fa|۱۵۵۷ (میلادی)|fi|1557|fo|1557|fr|1557|frr|1557|fur|1557|fy|1557|ga|1557|gan|1557年|gcr|1557|gd|1557|gl|1557|gv|1557|he|1557|hi|१५५७|hr|1557.|ht|1557 (almanak jilyen)|hu|1557|hy|1557|ia|1557|id|1557|ilo|1557|io|1557|is|1557|it|1557|ja|1557年|jv|1557|ka|1557|kaa|1557|kk|1557 жыл|ko|1557년|krc|1557 джыл|ksh|Joohr 1557|la|1557|lb|1557|lfn|1557|lij|1557|lmo|1557|lt|1557 m.|lv|1557. gads|mai|१५५७|map_bms|1557|mdf|1557|mg|1557|mhr|1557|mi|1557|min|1557|mk|1557|mr|इ.स. १५५७|mrj|1557 и|ms|1557|my|၁၅၅၇|mzn|۱۵۵۷|nah|1557|nap|1557|nds|1557|new|सन् १५५७|nl|1557|nn|1557|no|1557|nrm|1557|nso|1557|oc|1557|or|୧୫୫୭|os|1557-æм аз|pl|1557|pnb|1557|pt|1557|qu|1557|ro|1557|ru|1557 год|rue|1557|sa|१५५७|sah|1557|scn|1557|sd|1557ع|se|1557|sh|1557.|shn|1557|simple|1557|sk|1557|sl|1557|smn|1557|sq|1557|sr|1557|su|1557|sv|1557|sw|1557|ta|1557|tg|Соли 1557|th|พ.ศ. 2100|tk|1557|tl|1557|tly|1557|tr|1557|tt|1557 ел|uk|1557|ur|1557ء|uz|1557|vec|1557|vi|1557|vls|1557|wa|1557|war|1557|wuu|1557年|xmf|1557|yi|1557|zea|1557|zh|1557年|zh_min_nan|1557 nî|zh_yue|1557年|qid=Q6595}}), land surveys and destruction of halls by {{ill|Ōtomo Sōrin|Q1185032|qid=Q1185032}} caused further decline; it is said that although there were once 370 monks’ quarters at its height, this had fallen to 25 by the early modern period <ref name="地名"/>.

Later, in the early modern period, the Kobayakawa and Kuroda clans revived it as a Shugendō training ground for yamabushi <ref name="地名"/>. However, due in part to the fire of Kan’ei 18 (1641), most temple buildings were lost, and by the mid-Edo period most surrounding monks’ quarters had disappeared <ref name="地名"/>. The remaining Buddhist facilities were completely eliminated during the Meiji anti-Buddhist movement <ref name="角川"/>.

== Anime Pilgrimage Site ==
* {{ill|Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba|Q24862683|qid=Q24862683}}: Although the precise relationship has not been clarified by Koyoharu Gotouge or Shueisha, the shrine has attracted attention as a possible pilgrimage site for “Demon Slayer” due to several common points: it shares the surname “Kamado” with the protagonist Kamado Tanjiro; the shrine is associated with sealing the {{ill|Kimon|Q11673539|qid=Q11673539}} of {{ill|Dazaifu (government)|Q144845|qid=Q144845}}; ascetics training on Mount Hōman wear garments with a {{ill|Check (pattern)|Q14290457|qid=Q14290457}} matching Tanjiro’s {{ill|Haori|Q1503993|qid=Q1503993}}; there is a grave of a swordsmith named Kongōbei; and the author {{ill|Koyoharu Gotouge|Q24865213|qid=Q24865213}} is from Fukuoka Prefecture. Owned by Dazaifu Tenmangū. Designated April 1, 1982 <ref name="狛犬"/>.
* Tangible Folk Cultural Properties
** Materials related to Mount Hōman mountain worship  
**: A total of 307 items held by the shrine, including ritual implements, talismans, votive offerings, paintings, and records <ref name="信仰"/>. Evaluated as valuable materials related to ancient Mount Hōman worship <ref name="信仰"/>. Among them, the Sanskrit-inscribed sacred mirrors were donated in Kan’ei 18 (1641) by {{ill|Tadayuki Kuroda|Q11678600|qid=Q11678600}}, second lord of the Fukuoka Domain, representing the three deities of Kamado Shrine: Hōman-gū, Seibō-gū, and Hachiman-gū (the Hōman-gū mirror was lost in 1853) <ref name="信仰"/>. The Seibō-gū and Hachiman-gū mirrors are each just under 45 cm in diameter and 0.7 cm thick <ref name="信仰"/>. Designated February 20, 1962; additional designation and name change on March 18, 2011 <ref name="信仰"/>.

== On-Site Information ==
**Location**
* Upper Shrine: Kitadani, {{ill|Dazaifu, Fukuoka|Q728218|qid=Q728218}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258|qid=Q123258}} – summit of Mount Hōman.
* Lower Shrine: 883 Gokuyadani, Uchiyama, Dazaifu City, Fukuoka Prefecture

**Access (to the Lower Shrine)**
* Bus: From {{ill|Dazaifu Station|Q5243657|qid=Q5243657}} on the {{ill|Dazaifu Line|Q5243658|qid=Q5243658}}, take the {{ill|Mahoroba-gō|Q11278478|qid=Q11278478}} Uchiyama Line, get off at the terminal “Uchiyama,” then walk a short distance.
* Car: About 8 km from {{ill|Dazaifu interchange|Q1575734|qid=Q1575734}} on the {{ill|Kyushu Expressway|Q1060803|qid=Q1060803}}.
** Paid parking available

**Nearby**
* Uchizan Castle Ruins
* Hōman Castle Ruins
